name: Provide daily inpatient medical and nursing care
summary: This process covers one patient's stay on a medicine unit, from arriving with a bed assignment to leaving home, to long-term care or rehabilitation, to intensive care or to end-of-life care. Hospitalists see the patient each day and write orders, registered and practical nurses assess and treat the patient every shift, personal support workers give personal care, and a charge nurse runs daily discharge rounds. Most patients are frail older adults with several conditions, so plans change daily, orders pass through clerks, scanners and pharmacy, and stays grow when a patient no longer needs acute care but waits for a long-term care bed.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation with about 300 inpatient medicine beds run by a hospitalist group, mixed RN/RPN nursing and a hospital information system with partly paper or scanned orders.
baseline.notes: One case is one stay on a medicine unit. One loop of steps s08-s14 is one hospital day. Medication passes are documented separately in med-medication-administration, so nursing minutes here exclude them.

unit_of_work: one inpatient stay on a medicine unit
trigger: An admitted patient is given a medicine bed by patient flow, usually from the emergency department and sometimes on step-down from intensive care or repatriation from a tertiary hospital.
end_state: The patient is discharged home, transferred to long-term care or rehabilitation, moved to intensive care, or referred to end-of-life care, and the bed is released.

volume.seasonality: Higher from December to March with influenza, RSV and, in 2020-2022, COVID-19 waves; lower in summer.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate. Cross-check: about 300 medicine beds at 97% occupancy give about 8,850 patient days a month, which at 1,150 stays means a mean stay of about 7.7 days including ALC days, consistent with src1 (median acute stay 4.6 days, ALC on 22% of bed-days).

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Copied from the organisation file: occupancy above 100% in winter with unfunded surge beds; the corporation opened 12-bed and 40-bed field hospitals in 2020.

Author's estimate: about 300 medicine beds covered by hospitalists carrying 18-25 patients each on weekdays, with weekend and evening admitting shifts; 24 FTE of the 40 hospitalists' time on this process.

roles.title: Consultant specialist (internal medicine, cardiology, nephrology, oncology and others)

evidence.note: Consult time on medicine inpatients only; most specialist time is in clinics and procedures.

RN time on this process excludes medication passes, which are documented in med-medication-administration. The 430 RN headcount covers about 300 medicine beds plus CCC, rehab and field hospital beds and includes many part-time staff.
RPN time excluding medication passes; RPNs carry the more stable patients in a mixed RN/RPN model.
Personal support workers on medicine units at roughly one per 10-12 patients on day and evening shifts.
Unit clerks on about 10 medicine units, 07:00-23:00, seven days.

The organisation file has no charge nurse for inpatient units. Ontario medicine units of 30-40 beds run a charge or resource RN on every shift who assigns patients, takes bed calls and leads daily discharge rounds; about 10 units across three sites at two shifts a day gives about 60 heads (author's estimate). Cost set equal to the emergency charge nurse.
Patient care managers spend part of their week on bed escalations, staffing gaps and family concerns for individual stays.
Director time on escalated stays (long ALC waits, complaints).

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Electronic bed board and patient flow dashboard
Pharmacy information system and automated dispensing cabinets
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Fax (referrals, requisitions and reports to community physicians)
Document imaging and scanning of paper chart forms
Home and community care referral portal (Health Partner Gateway)

steps.name: Accept bed assignment and assign a nurse
steps.description: The charge nurse sees the bed assignment on the electronic bed board or takes the call from patient flow, checks that the cleaned bed suits the patient (isolation, telemetry, falls risk) and assigns the patient to an RN or RPN whose workload can absorb a new admission.

error.defect_description: Patient assigned to a bed or nurse that does not fit isolation or acuity needs, found on arrival.

evidence.note: Author's description of common Ontario practice; bed allocation itself is in cs-bed-management.

steps.name: Prepare the unit chart and notify the team
steps.description: The unit clerk opens the admission in the hospital information system, prints labels and the paper chart forms still used on the unit, adds the patient to the unit census board and pages the admitting hospitalist that the patient has a bed.

error.defect_description: Wrong attending physician or missing allergy band information on the chart.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of clerk work per admission.

steps.name: Take handover report from the sending unit
steps.description: The receiving nurse takes a structured verbal report (SBAR) by phone from the emergency or ICU nurse: diagnosis, vital signs, lines, medications given, isolation status, code status and outstanding tests, and notes questions to check on arrival.

error.defect_description: Pending test or medication given in the ED not passed on.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: information transfer at care transitions

evidence.note: ROP on information transfer at transitions; times are the author's estimate. The wait is the time the sending nurse takes to call while busy with other patients.

steps.name: Receive the patient and complete the admission nursing assessment
steps.description: When the porter brings the patient, the nurse confirms identity with two identifiers, takes vital signs, does a head-to-toe assessment, screens falls risk, skin (Braden score) and delirium, records belongings and allergies and starts the nursing care plan in the electronic record.
outputs: falls and pressure injury risk scores

error.defect_description: Risk screen incomplete, so falls or pressure injury precautions are not started.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROPs: client identification, falls prevention, pressure ulcer prevention

evidence.note: Screens required by the ROPs; minutes are the author's estimate. Wait covers porter transport from the ED and late bed cleaning.

steps.name: Take the best possible medication history
steps.description: The nurse interviews the patient and family about every home medication, checks pill bottles or the community pharmacy list, and where the patient cannot say, phones or faxes the community pharmacy, then records the list on the medication reconciliation form.

error.defect_description: A home medication or dose is missed from the list.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: medication reconciliation at care transitions (BPMH at admission)

evidence.note: ROP requires a BPMH at admission; in many community hospitals the ED or a pharmacy technician starts it. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hospitalist reviews the patient and writes admission orders
steps.description: The hospitalist reads the ED record and results, sees the patient, compares the BPMH with the admission medication orders, decides which home medications to continue, and writes or revises orders for medications, diet, activity, monitoring, tests and code status.

error.defect_description: Unintended medication discrepancy or omitted VTE prophylaxis order.

control.basis: Ontario Public Hospitals Act, Regulation 965: treatment only on the written order of a physician or other authorized practitioner

evidence.note: Many admitting hospitalists see the patient in the ED; this step is the review on the unit. Wait reflects the hospitalist working through several new admissions.

steps.name: Transcribe and send admission orders
steps.description: The unit clerk flags new orders, enters or requisitions tests, books imaging, scans or faxes medication orders to pharmacy and sends diet orders to food services; the nurse then checks the transcription against the signed orders.

error.defect_description: Order transcribed wrongly or missed.

evidence.note: Paper and scanned orders were still common in Ontario community hospitals in 2019-2022; only 19% of Canadian hospitals had operational CPOE in 2020/21 (CSHP survey, not cited here). Author's estimate.

steps.name: Shift handover and morning nursing assessment
steps.description: At the start of each day, the oncoming nurse takes bedside handover, reviews overnight events and new results, assesses the patient, takes vital signs and an early-warning score, and updates the plan for the day. The bed stays occupied for the whole hospital day.

error.defect_description: A change in condition is missed at handover.

evidence.note: One loop of s08-s14 is one hospital day. The wait is the overnight gap to the next morning; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Give morning personal care
steps.description: The personal support worker helps the patient wash, toilet, dress and get to a chair, sets up breakfast and helps with eating, repositions bed-bound patients and reports changes in skin, intake or behaviour to the nurse.

error.defect_description: Repositioning or intake not done or not recorded.

evidence.note: Most medicine patients are frail older adults (median age 73, src1) needing help with daily activities; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hospitalist daily review and rounds
steps.description: The hospitalist reviews overnight notes, vital signs, lab and imaging results, sees and examines the patient, writes a progress note, adjusts medication and test orders and decides whether a specialist consult is needed.

error.defect_description: Abnormal result not acted on the same day.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a hospitalist census of 18-25 patients a day. Wait is the patient's place in the rounding order.

steps.name: Process the day's new orders
steps.description: The unit clerk picks up the new orders, enters lab and imaging requisitions, calls or emails for bookings, scans medication orders to pharmacy and updates the census board with tests and expected discharge date.

error.defect_description: Order missed or entered on the wrong patient.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Deliver daytime nursing care
steps.description: The nurse carries out treatments and monitoring through the day: wound care, IV and line care, intake and output, blood glucose checks, mobilising, collecting specimens, preparing the patient for tests off the unit and documenting assessments and care in the record.

error.defect_description: Treatment or monitoring missed because of workload.

evidence.note: Nursing minutes excluding medication passes, which make up about a quarter of nurse time (src4) and sit in med-medication-administration. Author's estimate.

steps.name: Daily discharge planning rounds
steps.description: The charge nurse leads a short standing meeting with the nurse, social worker, physiotherapist, occupational therapist and discharge planner, confirms the expected discharge date, flags barriers such as home care or a long-term care bed, and records actions on the whiteboard and bed board.

error.defect_description: Expected discharge date not updated, so home care or family transport is arranged late.

evidence.note: Daily bullet or discharge rounds are common Ontario practice; three minutes per patient is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Evening and night nursing care and reassessment
steps.description: The evening and night nurse reassesses the patient, monitors vital signs and early-warning scores, manages pain, toileting and confusion, documents the shift and decides with the hospitalist on call whether the patient is deteriorating, ready for discharge, waiting for another setting or needs comfort care.

error.defect_description: Deterioration recognised late at night.

next.condition: still needs acute care: next hospital day
no longer needs acute care but cannot go home (ALC)
goals of care change to comfort care

evidence.note: Daily exit probabilities set so that the acute stay has a median of about 4.6 days with an interquartile range of about 2.5-8.6, ALC on about 11% of stays, in-hospital death or comfort care about 7% and ICU transfer about 3% (src1 reports ICU use 9.9% including ICU admissions from the ED). Night nursing minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Specialist consultation
steps.description: The consultant specialist (cardiology, nephrology, gastroenterology or another service) reviews the chart, sees the patient, writes recommendations and sometimes books a procedure, then the hospitalist adopts the recommendations as orders.

error.defect_description: Recommendation not converted into an order.

evidence.note: Daily consult probability of 6% gives about 30% of stays with at least one consult; author's estimate. Wait reflects consultants seeing inpatients between clinics.

steps.name: Write the discharge order and summary
steps.description: At morning rounds the hospitalist confirms the patient is ready, writes the discharge order and prescriptions, completes discharge medication reconciliation and dictates or types the discharge summary for the family physician.

error.defect_description: Discharge medication discrepancy or incomplete summary.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROP: medication reconciliation at care transitions (discharge)

evidence.note: ROP covers reconciliation at discharge. The wait is the overnight gap between the night decision and morning rounds; author's estimate.

steps.name: Discharge teaching and handover to home
steps.description: The nurse reviews the medication list and warning signs with the patient and family, removes IV lines, confirms home care start dates and follow-up appointments, gives the written instructions and copies of prescriptions, and documents the discharge.

error.defect_description: Patient leaves without understanding a medication change.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the stay and release the bed
steps.description: Once the family arrives, the unit clerk discharges the patient in the ADT module, which updates the bed board and sends a cleaning request; the clerk files remaining paper forms for scanning.

error.defect_description: Discharge not entered promptly, so the bed shows occupied.

evidence.note: Wait is for family pick-up or transport; author's estimate.

steps.name: Designate the patient as alternate level of care
steps.description: The hospitalist documents that the patient no longer needs acute care but cannot be discharged safely, records the ALC designation and the planned destination (long-term care, rehabilitation or convalescent care), and the discharge planner starts the application.

error.defect_description: ALC designation recorded late, understating ALC days.

control.basis: Provincial ALC designation guidance and CIHI Discharge Abstract Database ALC reporting

evidence.note: ALC on 12.4% of GIM admissions and 22% of bed-days (src1); 5.8% of all Canadian stays include ALC days (src2).

steps.name: Care for the patient while waiting for placement
steps.description: Each day the nurse and personal support worker give care, mobilisation and meals to the ALC patient in an acute bed, while the discharge planner and home and community care coordinator wait for a long-term care or rehabilitation bed offer.

error.defect_description: Functional decline from limited mobilisation while waiting.

next.condition: still waiting for a bed offer

evidence.note: Daily offer probability of 8% gives a mean of about 12.5 ALC days per ALC patient, consistent with 12.4% of admissions accounting for 22% of bed-days in src1. Care minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Transfer the patient to long-term care or rehabilitation
steps.description: The nurse prepares the transfer package (medication list, care plan, recent notes), gives report by phone to the receiving home or unit, books non-urgent patient transport and sends the patient with belongings and medications.

error.defect_description: Medication list in the transfer package is out of date.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada ROPs: information transfer and medication reconciliation at care transitions

evidence.note: Wait covers the receiving home's admission time and transport booking; author's estimate.

steps.name: Escalate deterioration to the rapid response team
steps.description: When the early-warning score or the nurse's concern triggers escalation, the nurse calls the rapid response team, stays at the bedside giving oxygen and monitoring, and gives report; the team either stabilises the patient on the ward or moves them to intensive care.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: The rapid response visit itself is in med-rapid-response; the 40% ICU transfer share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Change goals of care and refer to palliative care
steps.description: The hospitalist meets the patient and family to discuss prognosis, records a change to comfort-focused care, stops non-beneficial tests and treatments, writes symptom-control orders and refers to the palliative care team.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: In-hospital death 6.5% of GIM admissions (src1). Wait is for family to gather; author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Alternate level of care wait
exceptions.description: The patient no longer needs acute care but cannot go home; the stay continues in an acute bed until a long-term care or rehabilitation bed is offered, often for weeks.

exceptions.name: Specialist consultation
exceptions.description: The hospitalist asks a specialist to see the patient; recommendations arrive later the same day or the next day.

exceptions.name: Deterioration on the ward
exceptions.description: The nurse calls the rapid response team; about four in ten such patients go to intensive care.

exceptions.name: Comfort care
exceptions.description: Goals of care change and the patient is referred to end-of-life care.

benchmarks.unit: days from admission to discharge (acute portion for p50)
benchmarks.population: General internal medicine admissions, 7 Toronto-area hospitals, 2010-2015

evidence.note: p50 is the median acute length of stay in src1 (IQR 2.5-8.6). p90 is the author's extrapolation from that interquartile range plus ALC days; src1 does not report a 90th percentile.

benchmarks.unit: share of GIM admissions with ALC days

evidence.note: ALC days were 22.0% of GIM bed-days.

benchmarks.unit: share of GIM admissions with an ICU stay

evidence.note: Includes ICU stays before arrival on the medicine unit.

benchmarks.population: Medical, surgical and ICU nurses, one US tertiary hospital, 2005

evidence.note: Used to remove medication passes from the nursing minutes in this file.

pain_points.description: Patients who no longer need acute care wait in acute beds for long-term care or rehabilitation, holding a fifth of medicine bed-days and backing up admissions in the emergency department.

evidence.note: ALC on 22.0% of GIM bed-days.

pain_points.description: Discharge decisions made at night or late morning wait for the next hospitalist round and for family transport, so beds are released in the afternoon after the morning surge of ED admissions.

evidence.note: Author's observation of common practice.

pain_points.description: Orders pass from the hospitalist to the clerk, scanner and pharmacy queue, so a medication change made on morning rounds can take hours to reach the medication record.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; see the pharmacy order verification workflow for measured turnaround times.

pain_points.description: Handover between ED and ward nurses is verbal and rushed, and pending results or medications already given are missed.

evidence.note: Information transfer at care transitions is an Accreditation Canada ROP because of this risk.

sources.title: Patient characteristics, resource use and outcomes associated with general internal medicine hospital care: the General Medicine Inpatient Initiative (GEMINI) retrospective cohort study
sources.supports: 136,208 general internal medicine admissions at 7 Toronto hospitals 2010-2015: median age 73, median 6 comorbidities, median acute length of stay 4.6 days (IQR 2.5-8.6), ALC on 12.4% of admissions and 22.0% of bed-days, ICU use 9.9%, in-hospital death 6.5%, 30-day readmission 10.9%, discharged home 70.8%, nursing home or rehabilitation 18.9%; GIM is 38.8% of admissions from the ED; radiography 83.0%, CT 52.2%, transfusion 9.2% of admissions.

sources.title: Hospital stays in Canada, 2021-2022
sources.supports: About 2.9 million acute hospitalizations in 2021-2022; average acute length of stay 7.2 days; heart failure 9.2 days, COVID-19 10.1 days; 5.8% of stays included alternate level of care days.

sources.title: Required Organizational Practices 2021 Handbook
sources.publisher: Accreditation Canada (copy hosted by Vitalite Health Network)
sources.supports: Accreditation Canada ROPs include client identification with two identifiers, information transfer at care transitions, medication reconciliation at care transitions (best possible medication history at admission), concentrated electrolytes, heparin safety, high-alert medications, infusion pump safety, narcotics safety, falls prevention, pressure ulcer prevention and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

sources.title: Impact of Barcode Medication Administration Technology on How Nurses Spend Their Time On Clinical Care
sources.publisher: AMIA Annual Symposium Proceedings (Poon EG, Keohane C and others)
sources.supports: Time-motion study, 232 two-hour sessions on medical, surgical and intensive care units of a 735-bed hospital: nurses spent 26.5% of their time on medication administration before barcode administration and 24.5% after (not significant); direct care unrelated to medications 20.1% and 23.7%.

assumptions: Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage plus about 25-30% benefits and overhead). Physician costs are an equivalent hourly cost; hospitalists and consultants bill OHIP or are paid by stipend and are not on payroll.

Nursing minutes exclude medication passes (about a quarter of nurse time, src4), which are documented in hosp-med-medication-administration, so the labour here understates the full nursing cost of a stay.

The daily loop (s08-s14) is about 1,440 minutes of elapsed time. Daily exit probabilities (16% discharge-ready, 2.2% ALC, 1.5% deterioration, 1.3% comfort care) reproduce the GEMINI median and interquartile range of acute stay; real exit chances are higher on weekdays and lower on weekends.
Weekend discharges are fewer in practice; the model spreads exits evenly across days.
The organisation file has no inpatient charge nurse role; med_charge_nurse is added here (not_in_org_file).

The bed is tied up for each hospital day through the resource entries on s04, s08 and s20; mean bed-hours per stay in the simulation should be close to 300 beds x about 715 available hours / 1,150 stays (about 185 hours).
ICU transfer here covers only deterioration on the medicine unit (about 3% of stays); most of GEMINI's 9.9% ICU use happens before the patient reaches the unit.
The simulated median includes ALC and discharge-day waits, so it runs slightly above the GEMINI median of the acute portion alone.
